text: Two policemen are asked to account for two deaths, and the accounting takes the whole picture. Whether force was excessive is not a question a film can settle in one stroke; this one is built to arrive at it by increments, each new statement quietly revising the last. Made for television, it has to keep the case legible across interruptions, so the material comes in tested, self-contained blocks rather than one long unravelling. Crime stories about police usually pick a side in the first reel. Here the choice is deferred, and the men under suspicion stay colleagues throughout, subject to the same procedure they have spent their working lives applying to other people. That is the uncomfortable part. The investigation is competent, and competence is exactly what closes in on them.

A thirteen-year-old writes down two rules for middle school: stay cool, and make no friends. Chiaki Matsumoto has her reasons, elementary school having taught her what being available to other people costs, and Shin Togashi's film treats the policy as a policy rather than a phase to be waited out. Most of it is the maintenance: what it takes to keep a rule like that running inside a building designed for company. Then Kiki turns up, flamboyant, hard to place by age or by gender, and therefore outside the categories Chiaki has been sorting everyone into. The thaw is slow and it is not free. She built the walls for a reason, and trusting anyone again means agreeing that the reason has expired, which is a harder concession at thirteen than at any age after.

The fear comes secondhand: a boy at school tells Ali that his stepmother beats him, and from that afternoon Ali knows what a second wife is, before there is one. His father Ismaeil, widowed, raising Ali and his sister Sona, is being worked on by friends who think a man should not stay alone. The woman he marries, Astar, is a teacher, and she is kind to the children, which changes nothing at first. So a rumor and a person are set against each other inside one house, and the film gives the contest time rather than incident: hostility a child has to renew every morning, against an adult who declines to answer it in kind. The rooms are shared. The meals are shared. Ismaeil is stranded in the middle of his own household, having done the reasonable thing.

Itaewon, and a law student is spending his evenings in the wrong part of Seoul. He came out of a small village with a career already sketched for him; she works the bars, moves when she feels like it, and treats his devotion as one more thing that will not hold. Itaewon here is a workplace: shifts, customers, hours that belong to somebody else. The film follows her, which is its least obvious decision, and the chase runs from those clubs out of the country altogether, to the United States, the student trailing after and the degree receding behind him. Jang Gil-su pitches all of it high. Recklessness is treated as a position a person can actually hold rather than a symptom awaiting a cure, and the two hours go to whether either of them can survive at the other's speed.

One of them is climbing in Seoul; the other wants only to go home, and it is the second one who does the work. Yu-ra is after money and a name. Jun, who came from a town he would rather be in, spends the film assisting her ascent, absorbing her temper, making himself necessary to an ambition he does not share. Two hours and eight minutes is a long stretch to give someone else's career, and Kim Ho-sun uses it to look past the question of whether she arrives. What accumulates is the price of being useful: a person organized entirely around another person's future, calling it love, or duty, or nothing much. The industry that made this gave it the Baeksang for best film, which is a business finding its own likeness acceptable.

A boys' school team ran Argentine football for a decade, and half a century later a studio built a film to put it back on its feet. The reconstruction covers the Buenos Aires English High School and Alumni, the club its students formed, and Alejandro Watson Hutton, first president of the Argentine Football Association and, by this film's reckoning, the father of the game in the country. Filed as adventure as much as drama, which sets the register: ninety-five minutes played for speed and uplift rather than archival caution. It took the Silver Condor for best film. The men being remembered were recent enough in 1950 that some of the audience could have watched them play, and a picture made under those conditions is doing something other than history.

A river, a village on one bank, a UN base on the other: the geography does most of the film's arguing. Eon-rae is assaulted by soldiers of the UN forces, and the village answers by pushing her out, her and her son both, so she crosses the water to the brothel district that has grown up beside the camp and lives there in full view of the people who exiled her. The Korean War is the frame, but the eye stays on one settlement rather than a nation. That proximity is the method. Two hours of watching an old order take in what it cannot digest, cash and uniforms and unfamiliar goods, while insisting the damage came with the woman rather than with the war. Nothing is presented as exceptional. The ostracism runs on ordinary village logic, applied by neighbors, in daylight.

Command came to Mehdi Zeinoddin young, young enough that the fact is now inseparable from how he is remembered. Mehdi Shamohammadi narrows to one stretch of that war: Majnoon Island, during the Khaybar operation, inside a conflict that ran from 1980 to 1989. Made in 2023 under Owj Arts and Media Organization, it works from a settled national account rather than from contested memory, and it commemorates rather than interrogates; the martyr is a martyr before the first frame. What a film in that position can still do is scale. One island, one operation, one man given more authority than his years, and the pressure of that arithmetic on everyone standing downstream of his orders. It took the Crystal Simorgh for best film.

Ninety minutes, one marriage, and nothing wrong with it that could be named in court. The husband and wife are fond of each other and cannot get that across; the failure is not cruelty and not boredom exactly, but the way a settled routine takes over the job of speaking on their behalf. They are middle class and comfortable, which strips the story of every external excuse it might have leaned on. Enrique Carreras files it as comedy and drama at once, the harder assignment, since the laughs have to be built out of the same repetitions doing the damage. The trouble is small and it does not let up. Two people conduct an intimate life in a shared vocabulary neither of them can hear anymore, and the audience is left noticing what the couple cannot.

Any film about Yeonsan of Joseon has to decide early how much of the man to explain. Im Kwon-taek's runs just under two hours and stays inside the court, where the chain of command is short enough that a ruler's temperament becomes state policy without passing through anything that might slow it down. The pull is not the outline of the reign, which history fixed long ago, but the mechanics: an apparatus of officials, protocol and paperwork rearranging itself daily around one man's mood, the rearranging being the only work anyone gets done. It was named best film at the Grand Bell awards. Costume buys room to argue at full volume, five centuries clear of anyone still in a position to take offense.

In 1965 a Canadian crew went up on a napalm and strafing run and brought the footage home for television. Fifty-six minutes, shot entirely on location in South Vietnam, and the governing decision was to hand over the microphone: soldiers from the army, the marines, the air cavalry and the ARVN account for themselves, in their own words, at their own length, on why Communism has to be stopped where they are standing. Beryl Fox sets that against Saigon traffic and the ordinary daylight of village work. Nothing is narrated into shape. The camera goes where the units go, including to the bodies afterward, and the justifications are left standing exactly as the men speaking them built them, which is colder than any argument the CBC could have written around it.

A Buenos Aires studio put two hours and five minutes into the life of a Spanish composer in 1947, which says something about who the audience was and what it wanted from Europe. Isaac Albéniz appears first as a prodigy under a tyrannical father, and the picture's opening move is flight: out of the house, across the ocean, into whatever a gifted boy can build in America with no family behind him and no route back that does not run through his father. The return is the second half, the halls and the reputation and the attention that arrives with a reputation. Luis César Amadori keeps the two panels in tension. The prodigy was manufactured by the man he ran from, and no escape undoes the manufacturing, which is why the triumphs play with a chill under them.
